result_text:
### Research question
Is a camera-based "second-opinion" vision confirmation modality for SPARK (Action #28, Ch.6 future work, contingent on Action #27's resolved NPU/iGPU benchmarking) technically feasible? What architecture patterns exist in published IMU+vision multimodal fall-confirmation literature, what specifically does a vision second opinion catch that IMU-only misses, and do the compute requirements sanity-check against SPARK's already-benchmarked gateway headroom (NPU 383µs/window, Arc iGPU 200µs/window, Action #27 v52)?

### Bottom line
Yes, feasible, and well-supported. Published decision-level (late) IMU+RGB fusion work (Rehouma & Boukadoum, *Sensors* 2025) cuts false-positive rate from 11.3% (IMU-only) / 8.9% (vision-only) to 3.6% fused, at ~20 fps on **CPU-only** commodity hardware weaker than SPARK's gateway laptop — meaning SPARK's Acer Swift Go 16 (Core Ultra 7 155H, NPU+iGPU, currently spending only 200–383µs/window on the IMU CNN) has enormous headroom to spare for a second vision stream. The literature converges on two architecture families — mobile-robot-navigates-then-confirms, and stationary/room-camera decision-level fusion — and the latter is the correct fit for SPARK, since SPARK has no robot and already has a laptop gateway (§2.1 Layer 2) that could ingest a camera feed directly. Vision specifically corrects the failure mode SPARK's own Layer 1 hardware gate (simple 2.5g/300ms magnitude threshold, §2.5) is structurally prone to: abrupt-but-benign accelerometric impulses (quick sitting, dropped/bumped device, jumping) that spike magnitude without a real fall.

### Key findings

**Finding 1 — Decision-level IMU+vision fusion substantially cuts false positives without hurting sensitivity, on CPU-only hardware weaker than SPARK's gateway.**
- Evidence: N=16 healthy adults, waist-mounted IMU (50 Hz) + waist-height RGB camera at <5 lux (nighttime bedroom scenario), LOSO cross-validation, decision-level fusion (independent scores gated at threshold α=0.70). IMU-only (LSTM autoencoder): 90.3% acc, FPR 11.3%, AUC 0.931. Vision-only (Transformer over BlazePose 33-point 2D pose): 92.9% acc, FPR 8.9%, AUC 0.962. Fused: 97.2% acc, 97.8% recall, **FPR 3.6%**, AUC 0.989. End-to-end latency ≈50±4.7 ms/frame (~20 fps) on an **Intel Core i5-8265U, CPU-only, no GPU**, 8GB RAM.
- Source: Rehouma, H. & Boukadoum, M. "Fall Detection by Deep Learning-Based Bimodal Movement and Pose Sensing with Late Fusion." *Sensors* 25(19):6035, 2025. DOI: 10.3390/s25196035. Open access, PMC12526565.
- Confidence: **Established** (peer-reviewed, quantified methodology, statistically tested p<0.001).
- Relevance to SPARK: Directly grounds the Ch.6 feasibility claim. If a fused pipeline clears real-time budgets on an i5-8265U with *no* dedicated accelerator, it will clear them trivially on SPARK's Core Ultra 7 155H gateway, which already has NPU/iGPU capacity confirmed idle-fast (Action #27).

**Finding 2 — Vision correction targets exactly SPARK's own Layer-1 weak point: simple-threshold false positives from non-fall accelerometric impulses.**
- Evidence: The fusion paper's own error analysis attributes its FPR reduction to vision suppressing "false positives from inertial impulses (e.g., abrupt sitting)," while IMU compensates when vision is degraded (occlusion/darkness). This is corroborated independently: quick sitting and jumping are repeatedly cited as classic accelerometer-threshold false-positive triggers (MDPI Sensors 25(12):3632, 2025); dropped/picked-up objects and "diving into the sofa" are cited as real-world false-alarm causes in a continuously-running deployed system (SiFall, arXiv:2301.03773, false-alarm rate fell from 13.4%→1.4% only after continuous model personalization, i.e., threshold-only systems stay vulnerable to this class of event without a second signal).
- Source: Rehouma & Boukadoum (2025) §6.1; MDPI Sensors 25(12):3632 (2025); SiFall arXiv:2301.03773.
- Confidence: **Established** for the general IMU false-positive failure mode; **supported inference** that it applies identically to SPARK, since SPARK's Layer 1 (§2.5: |a|<2.5g for >300ms magnitude+duration gate) is the same class of simple-threshold algorithm, but this hasn't been empirically tested against SPARK's actual gate — Action #7's empirical threshold tuning is still open.
- Relevance to SPARK: A vision second opinion is complementary to SPARK's actual architecture (checks the cruder Layer-1 gate, not a redundant re-check of the CNN), strengthening the case for prioritizing this in Ch.6 over a vaguer "vision helps generally" framing.

**Finding 3 — Two dominant architecture patterns exist; the stationary/decision-fusion pattern (not the mobile-robot pattern) fits SPARK's locked design.**
- Evidence: Literature splits into (a) mobile-robot-navigates-to-location-then-vision-confirms (Sumiya 2015, Kinect, 80% acc; Kalinga 2020, Kinect, 92.5% acc/95.45% sens; Elwaly 2024, YOLOv7, 96% acc but requires subject 185–220cm from camera; Azghadi et al. 2025, chained IMU→RSSI-localize→robot-navigate→vision-confirm, 99.99% system-level accuracy by multiplying independently-reliable stages) and (b) stationary/room-camera decision-level fusion with no robot (Rehouma & Boukadoum 2025, above). A companion-robot approach using early/CNN-LSTM video-only confirmation (Liang et al. 2021) underperforms decision fusion at 84% accuracy. Early/input-level fusion (Qi et al. 2023, UP-Fall dataset, 99.9% binary accuracy) is reported as accurate but is flagged across multiple reviews as riskier than late fusion because it propagates modality-specific noise.
- Source: Azghadi et al., "A Privacy-Preserving Multi-Stage Fall Detection Framework with Semi-supervised Federated Learning and Robotic Vision Confirmation," arXiv:2507.10474 (2025), Table 1 + §3 (survey + own robot-based system); Rehouma & Boukadoum (2025) §2.4 (early-vs-late fusion discussion); Deep Neural Network-Based Double-Check Method (IEEE, D.-W. Lee et al., robot-mounted RGB "double-check" pattern).
- Confidence: **Established** (consistent pattern across independent groups/years).
- Relevance to SPARK: SPARK has no robot in its BOM/scope and already has a laptop gateway co-located as the sole compute (§2.1 Layer 2, locked v35). Ch.6 should scope this explicitly as *stationary-camera, decision-level fusion feeding the existing gateway pipeline* — not the mobile-robot pattern, which is architecturally out of scope. This is a design-framing recommendation for the thesis chapter, not a code/design deliverable (per this track's no-build boundary).

**Finding 4 — Compute cost for a vision stream is trivial against the already-benchmarked NPU/iGPU headroom; this is a sanity-check extrapolation, not a direct SPARK-hardware measurement.**
- Evidence: Even *unaccelerated CPU-only* lightweight pose models hit real-time on hardware weaker than SPARK's gateway: Lightweight OpenPose achieves 28 fps on an Intel NUC 6i7KYB (mobile i7, no NPU/discrete GPU); BlazePose+Transformer (Finding 1's paper) achieves ~20 fps end-to-end on a CPU-only i5-8265U. SPARK's gateway NPU (383µs/window, 2,610 windows/s) and Arc iGPU (200µs/window, 4,993 windows/s) are currently used only for the IMU CNN — both are 2–3 orders of magnitude faster per-inference than what these vision pipelines need per frame, and OpenVINO (already the toolkit SPARK uses for Action #27) has native, documented pose-estimation and object-detection benchmarks on Arc GPU/NPU hardware.
- Source: Osokin, "Real-Time 2D Multi-Person Pose Estimation on CPU: Lightweight OpenPose," arXiv:1811.12004; Rehouma & Boukadoum (2025) §6.2; Intel, "Unlocking the AI Power of Intel Arc GPU" whitepaper (OpenVINO pose-estimation benchmark category); SPARK_TRACKER.md v54 §1 Action #27 (internal baseline, HEAD 53f194d).
- Confidence: **Supported inference** — the headroom argument is sound and well-evidenced by proxy, but nobody has actually run a vision model through SPARK's real OpenVINO/gateway pipeline yet; this is an extrapolation from comparable hardware, not a direct SPARK-specific benchmark.
- Relevance to SPARK: Directly answers the task's "sanity-check feasibility" requirement — the compute case is strong enough to justify listing this as concrete (not speculative) Ch.6 future work, while flagging that an actual on-gateway benchmark, if ever run, would be the natural follow-up.

### Evidence table

| Finding | Evidence | Source | Confidence | SPARK implication |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Late fusion cuts FPR 11.3%/8.9%→3.6%, ~20fps CPU-only | N=16 LOSO, waist IMU+RGB, i5-8265U no GPU | Rehouma & Boukadoum, *Sensors* 25(19):6035, 2025 | Established | Feasibility baseline; SPARK's gateway is strictly more capable |
| Vision suppresses IMU's "abrupt sitting"/impulse false positives | Error analysis + independent false-alarm-cause studies | Rehouma & Boukadoum (2025) §6.1; MDPI Sensors 25(12):3632; SiFall arXiv:2301.03773 | Established (general); Supported inference (SPARK-specific) | Vision targets SPARK's actual Layer-1 weak point |
| Stationary decision-fusion > mobile-robot / early-fusion patterns for SPARK's fit | Cross-study architecture survey, accuracy comparison | Azghadi et al. arXiv:2507.10474 (2025) Table 1; IEEE double-check paper | Established | Ch.6 should scope as gateway-local late fusion, no robot |
| Vision compute is trivial vs. NPU/iGPU headroom | Comparable-hardware pose-model benchmarks | Osokin arXiv:1811.12004; Rehouma & Boukadoum (2025) §6.2; Intel Arc OpenVINO whitepaper | Supported inference | Justifies concrete (not speculative) Ch.6 framing; real on-gateway benchmark still open |

### Contradictions and limitations
- **Population mismatch (same caveat as SisFall/Track 3):** every cited fusion-accuracy figure comes from young/healthy adult volunteers under scripted/simulated falls (Rehouma & Boukadoum: N=16, mean age 42.1±4.8; Qi et al./UP-Fall: young adults) — not SPARK's elderly/Nepal-context target population. None of these numbers should be quoted as SPARK's expected performance.
- **Sensor-placement gap, not resolved by current evidence:** every fusion paper found uses a **waist/torso**-mounted IMU. SPARK's IMU is **wrist**-worn (§2.2, locked v29). Wrist accelerometer dynamics (incidental arm motion while seated, gesturing) differ from waist, so the demonstrated "abrupt sitting" false-positive suppression may transfer imperfectly to a wrist-worn gate. This is a genuinely open question, flagged as unresolved rather than assumed.
- **Compute claim is extrapolated, not measured on SPARK's actual hardware/pipeline** — flagged in Finding 4.
- **Camera coverage/placement constraints are real and unaddressed by SPARK's current scope:** cited systems need specific subject-to-camera distances (Elwaly 2024: 185–220cm) or single-camera FOV (falls outside frame are missed — the same "falls occur outside the home/closed spaces" critique the existing NLM notebook's SisFall source already raises against ambient/camera systems generally). A room-mounted single camera reintroduces the coverage/intrusiveness limitation that originally motivated SPARK's wearable-first design — worth an explicit sentence of tension/tradeoff in Ch.6, not silently glossed over.
- **Privacy framing is new territory:** Novelty Claim 3's "local, non-cloud" framing is about SHAP/compute location, not about camera presence — a vision second opinion doesn't violate Claim 3 as currently worded, but Ch.6 should say so explicitly rather than leave it implicit.

### Recommendation
List Action #28 in Ch.6 as concrete (evidence-backed), not speculative, future work, framed specifically as: **gateway-local, decision-level (late) fusion, stationary single-camera vision second opinion, contingent on Action #27's confirmed NPU/iGPU headroom** — explicitly not a mobile-robot system (no robot in SPARK's BOM) and not early/input-level fusion (literature-flagged as noisier, and structurally mismatched to SPARK's existing modular Layer-1→Layer-2 gate design). Flag two concrete open research questions for whoever eventually scopes this past Ch.6: (1) does the IMU-side false-positive-suppression benefit hold for a wrist-worn IMU, since no cited study tests that placement; (2) camera coverage/placement tradeoff vs. SPARK's original wearable-first, non-intrusive design rationale. No design or code produced — this track is research-memo only per task scope.

NLM notebook 2c00f5a4-98dc-4783-96d1-3682fa3cb516 checked first (per task instructions) — confirmed no existing camera/vision-fusion sources present; only a brief critique-in-passing within the SisFall dataset paper (Sucerquia et al. 2017, *Sensors* 17(1):198) noting ambient/camera systems are restrictive for elderly living outside closed spaces — used here as a limitation note, not new evidence.
summary: Track 13 done: camera-vision fall-confirmation fusion is feasible as Ch.6 future work. Late/decision-level fusion (not robot-based, not early fusion) is the right pattern; compute cost is trivial next to the already-benchmarked NPU/iGPU headroom. Key gaps: no cited fusion study uses wrist-worn IMU (all are waist), and cohorts are young/healthy, not SPARK's elderly/Nepal target — same population-mismatch caveat as SisFall.
